<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:Binet-representation}
Assume that \eqref{eq:distinct-characteristic-roots}--\eqref{eq:root-conditions}
hold. Then there exist unique coefficients
$
A_1,\ldots,A_k\in\mathbb{K}
$
such that
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:Binet-representation}
\mathrm{U}_n
=
\sum_{j=1}^{k}A_j\lambda_j^n,
\qquad n\geq0.
\end{equation}
Conversely, every sequence of the form \eqref{eq:Binet-representation}
satisfies the recurrence \eqref{eq:linear-recurrence}.
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
For every $j$, the sequence $(\lambda_j^n)_{n\geq0}$ satisfies
\eqref{eq:linear-recurrence} by \eqref{eq:geometric-recurrence}.
Therefore every sequence of the form
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:general-geometric-combination}
V_n
=
\sum_{j=1}^{k}A_j\lambda_j^n
\end{equation}
also satisfies \eqref{eq:linear-recurrence}.

It remains to choose the coefficients so that $V_n$ has the prescribed
initial data. Requiring
$
V_r=\mathrm{U}_r,
\qquad
r=0,\ldots,k-1,
$
gives the linear system
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:Vandermonde-system}
\begin{pmatrix}
1 & 1 & \cdots & 1\\
\lambda_1 & \lambda_2 & \cdots & \lambda_k\\
\lambda_1^2 & \lambda_2^2 & \cdots & \lambda_k^2\\
\vdots & \vdots & & \vdots\\
\lambda_1^{k-1} & \lambda_2^{k-1} & \cdots
& \lambda_k^{k-1}
\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}
A_1\\
A_2\\
\vdots\\
A_k
\end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
\mathrm{U}_0\\
\mathrm{U}_1\\
\vdots\\
\mathrm{U}_{k-1}
\end{pmatrix}.
\end{equation}
The coefficient matrix is the Vandermonde matrix associated with
$\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_k$, whose determinant is
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:Vandermonde-determinant}
\prod_{1\leq i<j\leq k}(\lambda_j-\lambda_i).
\end{equation}
By the distinct-root hypothesis, the quantity in
\eqref{eq:Vandermonde-determinant} is nonzero. Hence
\eqref{eq:Vandermonde-system} has a unique solution
$A_1,\ldots,A_k$.

The resulting sequence $(V_n)_{n\geq0}$ and $\mathrm{U}$ satisfy the same
order-$k$ recurrence and agree at the first $k$ indices. Uniqueness of
solutions of \eqref{eq:linear-recurrence} with prescribed initial data
therefore gives
$
V_n=\mathrm{U}_n,
\qquad n\geq0.
$
This proves \eqref{eq:Binet-representation}. The converse follows from
linearity and the fact that every geometric component
$\lambda_j^n$ satisfies the recurrence.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
\label{def:spectral-Binet-operator}
The spectral Binet operator associated with the recurrence sequence $\mathrm{U}$
is defined by
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:spectral-Binet-operator}
\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{U}}=\sum_{j=1}^{k}A_j\mathrm{T}_{\lambda_j}.
\end{equation}
Equivalently,
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:spectral-Binet-operator-explicit}
\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{U}}f(x)=\sum_{j=1}^{k}A_jf(\lambda_jx).
\end{equation}
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{prop:Binet-operator-linearity}
The operator $\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{U}}$ is linear on every vector space on which all the
dilations $\mathrm{T}_{\lambda_1},\ldots,\mathrm{T}_{\lambda_k}$ are defined.
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
Let $f,g$ belong to such a vector space and let
$\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb K$. Then
\begin{align*}
\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{U}}(\alpha f+\beta g)
&=
\sum_{j=1}^{k}
A_j\mathrm{T}_{\lambda_j}(\alpha f+\beta g) \\
&=
\sum_{j=1}^{k}
A_j
\left(
\alpha\mathrm{T}_{\lambda_j}f
+
\beta\mathrm{T}_{\lambda_j}g
\right) \\
&=
\alpha\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{U}}f
+
\beta\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{U}}g.
\end{align*}
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\label{prop:Binet-monomial-action}
For every $n\geq0$,
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:Binet-monomial-action}
\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{U}}x^n
=
\mathrm{U}_nx^n.
\end{equation}
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
Using \eqref{eq:dilation-characteristic-mode} and the Binet representation
\eqref{eq:Binet-representation-operator-section}, we obtain
\begin{align*}
\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{U}}x^n
=
\sum_{j=1}^{k}
A_j\mathrm{T}_{\lambda_j}x^n 
=
\sum_{j=1}^{k}
A_j\lambda_j^n x^n 
=
\left(
\sum_{j=1}^{k}A_j\lambda_j^n
\right)x^n 
=
\mathrm{U}_nx^n.
\end{align*}
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
\label{cor:Binet-operator-recovery}
The action of $\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{U}}$ on the monomial basis uniquely determines the
sequence $\mathrm{U}$.
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
For every $n\geq0$, equation
\eqref{eq:Binet-monomial-action} uniquely determines $\mathrm{U}_n$ as the
scalar satisfying
$
\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{U}}x^n=\mathrm{U}_nx^n.
$
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- definition-2: body_md -->
\label{def:U-derivative}
The $\mathrm{U}$-derivative associated with the recurrence sequence $\mathrm{U}$ is
the operator
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:U-derivative-operator}
\mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{U}}
=
M_{x^{-1}}\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{U}}.
\end{equation}
Hence
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:U-derivative-explicit}
\mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{U}}f(x)
=
\frac{1}{x}
\sum_{j=1}^{k}A_jf(\lambda_jx).
\end{equation}
<!-- end definition-2 -->
<!-- proposition-3: body_md -->
\label{prop:U-derivative-linearity}
The operator $\mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{U}}$ is linear on its domain.
<!-- end proposition-3 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
Follows from Definition \ref{def:U-derivative} and Proposition \ref{prop:Binet-monomial-action}.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:fundamental-monomial-identity}
For every $n\geq0$,
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:fundamental-monomial-identity}
\mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{U}}x^n
=
\mathrm{U}_nx^{n-1}.
\end{equation}
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
Using Definition~\ref{def:U-derivative}, we have
\begin{align*}
\mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{U}}x^n
=
\frac{1}{x}
\sum_{j=1}^{k}
A_j(\lambda_jx)^n 
=
\left(
\sum_{j=1}^{k}
A_j\lambda_j^n
\right)x^{n-1}.
\end{align*}
By the Binet representation,
$
\sum_{j=1}^{k}A_j\lambda_j^n
=
\mathrm{U}_n,
$
and hence
$
\mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{U}}x^n
=
\mathrm{U}_nx^{n-1}.
$
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- proposition-4: body_md -->
\label{prop:U-derivative-polynomials}
Let $f(x)=\sum_{n=0}^{N}c_nx^n$. Then
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:U-derivative-polynomial}
\mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{U}}f(x)
=
\sum_{n=0}^{N}c_n\mathrm{U}_nx^{n-1}.
\end{equation}
Equivalently,
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:U-derivative-polynomial-separated}
\mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{U}}f(x)
=
c_0\mathrm{U}_0x^{-1}
+
\sum_{n=1}^{N}c_n\mathrm{U}_nx^{n-1}.
\end{equation}
<!-- end proposition-4 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
By linearity and Theorem~\ref{thm:fundamental-monomial-identity},
\begin{align*}
\mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{U}}f(x)
=
\mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{U}}
\left(
\sum_{n=0}^{N}c_nx^n
\right) 
=
\sum_{n=0}^{N}
c_n\mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{U}}x^n 
=
\sum_{n=0}^{N}
c_n\mathrm{U}_nx^{n-1}.
\end{align*}
Separating the term $n=0$ gives
\eqref{eq:U-derivative-polynomial-separated}.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- corollary-2: body_md -->
\label{cor:polynomial-invariance}
The polynomial algebra $\mathbb K[x]$ is invariant under
$\mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{U}}$ if and only if $\mathrm{U}_0=0$
<!-- end corollary-2 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
Suppose first that $\mathrm{U}_0=0$. Then
\eqref{eq:U-derivative-polynomial-separated} becomes
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:U-derivative-polynomial-Ward-form}
\mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{U}}f(x)
=
\sum_{n=1}^{N}c_n\mathrm{U}_nx^{n-1},
\end{equation}
which belongs to $\mathbb K[x]$. Hence
$
\mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{U}}\bigl(\mathbb K[x]\bigr)
\subseteq
\mathbb K[x].
$

Conversely, assume
$
\mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{U}}\bigl(\mathbb K[x]\bigr)
\subseteq
\mathbb K[x].
$
Since $1\in\mathbb K[x]$, equation
\eqref{eq:U-derivative-constant} implies that
$
\mathrm{U}_0x^{-1}\in\mathbb K[x].
$
This is possible only if $\mathrm{U}_0=0$.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- proposition-5: body_md -->
\label{prop:recovery-recurrence-from-DU}
The action of $\mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{U}}$ on the monomial basis uniquely determines
$\mathrm{U}_0,\mathrm{U}_1,\mathrm{U}_2,\ldots$.
<!-- end proposition-5 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
For every $n\geq0$,
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:recovery-coefficient}
\mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{U}}x^n
=
\mathrm{U}_nx^{n-1}.
\end{equation}
Therefore $\mathrm{U}_n$ is precisely the coefficient of $x^{n-1}$ in
$\mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{U}}x^n$, and the complete sequence is recovered from the monomial
action of the operator.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- corollary-3: body_md -->
\label{cor:equality-U-derivatives}
Let $\mathrm{U}=(\mathrm{U}_n)_{n\geq0}$ and $\mathrm{V}=(\mathrm{V}_n)_{n\geq0}$
be recurrence sequences for which the corresponding operators
$\mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{U}}$ and $\mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{V}}$ are defined. If
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:equality-operators-monomials}
\mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{U}}x^n
=
\mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{V}}x^n
\qquad
\text{for every }n\geq0,
\end{equation}
then
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:equality-recurrence-sequences}
\mathrm{U}_n=\mathrm{V}_n
\qquad
\text{for every }n\geq0.
\end{equation}
<!-- end corollary-3 -->
<!-- definition-3: body_md -->
\label{def:ward-regime} 
A recurrence sequence \(\mathrm{U}\) is said to belong to the \emph{Ward regime} if 
\begin{equation} \label{eq:ward-regime} 
\mathrm{U}_0=0. 
\end{equation}
<!-- end definition-3 -->
<!-- definition-4: body_md -->
\label{def:nonward-regime} 
A recurrence sequence \(\mathrm{U}\) is said to belong to the \emph{non-Ward regime} if \begin{equation} \label{eq:nonward-regime} \mathrm{U}_0\neq0. \end{equation}
<!-- end definition-4 -->
<!-- proposition-6: body_md -->
\label{prop:ward-characterization} 
The following statements are equivalent: 
\begin{enumerate} 
\item \(\mathrm{U}_0=0\); 
\item \(\mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{U}}(1)=0\); 
\item \(\mathbb K[x]\) is invariant under \(\mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{U}}\). 
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-6 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
The equivalence between (1) and (2) follows immediately from \eqref{eq:Du-on-constant-recall}. The equivalence between (1) and (3) was established in Corollary~\ref{cor:polynomial-invariance}. Indeed, \[ \mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{U}}(\mathbb K[x]) \subseteq \mathbb K[x] \] holds precisely when \(\mathrm{U}_0=0. \)
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{thm:iterates-monomials}
Let $n\geq 0$, and let $m$ be an integer such that
$
0\leq m\leq n.
$
Then
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:iterates-monomials}
\mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{U}}^{m}x^n
=
\left(
\prod_{j=0}^{m-1}\mathrm{U}_{n-j}
\right)x^{n-m}.
\end{equation}
For $m=0$, the product in \eqref{eq:iterates-monomials} is understood
to be the empty product and hence equal to $1$.
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
We proceed by induction on $m$. For $m=0$, the empty-product convention gives
\begin{equation}
\mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{U}}^{0}x^n
=
x^n
=
\left(
\prod_{j=0}^{-1}\mathrm{U}_{n-j}
\right)x^n,
\end{equation}
so \eqref{eq:iterates-monomials} holds. For $m=1$, the formula reduces to $\mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{U}} x^n=\mathrm{U}_nx^{n-1}$, which is precisely the fundamental monomial identity. Now suppose that, for some integer $m$ with $1\leq m<n$,
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:iteration-induction-hypothesis}
\mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{U}}^{m}x^n
=
\left(
\prod_{j=0}^{m-1}\mathrm{U}_{n-j}
\right)x^{n-m}.
\end{equation}
Applying $\mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{U}}$ to both sides of
\eqref{eq:iteration-induction-hypothesis} and using linearity, we obtain
\begin{align*}
\mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{U}}^{m+1}x^n
=
\mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{U}}
\left[
\left(
\prod_{j=0}^{m-1}\mathrm{U}_{n-j}
\right)x^{n-m}
\right]
=
\left(
\prod_{j=0}^{m-1}\mathrm{U}_{n-j}
\right)
\mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{U}} x^{n-m}.
\end{align*}
Since $m<n$, we have $n-m\geq1$, and the fundamental monomial
identity gives
\begin{equation}
\mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{U}} x^{n-m}
=
\mathrm{U}_{n-m}x^{n-m-1}.
\end{equation}
Therefore,
\begin{align*}
\mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{U}}^{m+1}x^n
=
\left(
\prod_{j=0}^{m-1}\mathrm{U}_{n-j}
\right)
\mathrm{U}_{n-m}x^{n-m-1}
=
\left(
\prod_{j=0}^{m}\mathrm{U}_{n-j}
\right)
x^{n-(m+1)}.
\end{align*}
This is exactly \eqref{eq:iterates-monomials} with $m$ replaced by
$m+1$. Hence the result follows by induction for every
$0\leq m\leq n$.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- corollary-4: body_md -->
\label{cor:complete-monomial-descent}
For every $n\geq1$, 
\begin{equation} 
\mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{U}}^n x^n = \mathrm{U}_n\mathrm{U}_{n-1}\cdots\mathrm{U}_1. 
\end{equation}
<!-- end corollary-4 -->
<!-- corollary-5: body_md -->
\label{cor:termination-degree-zero}
Suppose $\mathrm{U}_0=0.$ Then, for every $n\geq0$, 
$\mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{U}}^{n+1}x^n=0.$ Consequently, $\mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{U}}^m x^n=0,$ for $m>n. $
<!-- end corollary-5 -->
<!-- proposition-7: body_md -->
\label{prop:iterates-polynomials} 
Assume that $\mathrm{U}_0=0$. Let $f(x) = \sum_{n=0}^{N}c_nx^n$. 
Then, for every integer \(m\) satisfying \( 0\leq m\leq N, \) we have 
\begin{equation} \label{eq:iterates-polynomials} 
\mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{U}}^{m}f(x) = \sum_{n=m}^{N} c_n \left( \prod_{j=0}^{m-1}\mathrm{U}_{n-j} \right) x^{n-m}. 
\end{equation} 
For \(m=0\), the product is understood to be empty and equal to \(1\).
<!-- end proposition-7 -->
<!-- corollary-6: body_md -->
\label{cor:degree-lowering} 
Assume that \(\mathrm{U}_0=0\), and let \( f\in\mathbb K[x] \) satisfy \( \deg f\leq N. \) Then, for every \(m\) with \( 0\leq m\leq N, \) \begin{equation} \label{eq:degree-lowering} \deg\bigl(\mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{U}}^{m}f\bigr) \leq N-m, \end{equation} whenever \(\mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{U}}^{m}f\neq0\).
<!-- end corollary-6 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
\label{thm:local-nilpotence} 
Assume that $\mathrm{U}_0=0$. Then \(\mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{U}}\) is locally nilpotent on \(\mathbb K[x]\). More precisely, for every \(N\geq0\), 
\begin{equation} \label{eq:nilpotence-on-PN} 
\mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{U}}^{N+1}\big|_{\mathcal P_N} = 0. \end{equation} Equivalently, if \(f\in\mathbb K[x] \) satisfies \( \deg f\leq N, \) then 
\begin{equation} \label{eq:local-nilpotence} 
\mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{U}}^{N+1}f = 0. 
\end{equation}
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
Let \[ f(x) = \sum_{n=0}^{N}c_nx^n. \] For every monomial appearing in \(f\), Corollary~\ref{cor:termination-degree-zero} gives \( \mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{U}}^{n+1}x^n=0. \) Since \(N+1\geq n+1, \) it follows that \( \mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{U}}^{N+1}x^n=0\), \(0\leq n\leq N. \) Therefore 
\begin{align} 
\mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{U}}^{N+1}f &= \sum_{n=0}^{N} c_n \mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{U}}^{N+1}x^n= 0. 
\end{align} Hence \[ \mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{U}}^{N+1}\big|_{\mathcal P_N} = 0. \] Since every polynomial belongs to some finite-dimensional space \(\mathcal P_N\), the operator \(\mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{U}}\) is locally nilpotent on \(\mathbb K[x]\).
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- definition-5: body_md -->
\label{def:spectral-increments} 
For every index \(j\in\{1,\ldots,k\}\), define the spectral increment of a function \(h\) relative to \(\lambda_r\) by 
\begin{equation} \label{eq:spectral-increment-f} 
\Delta_{j,r}h = T_{\lambda_j}h - T_{\lambda_r}h. 
\end{equation}
<!-- end definition-5 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
\label{rem:vanishing-spectral-increments} Two increments vanish identically: \begin{equation} \label{eq:vanishing-increments} \Delta_{r,r}f=0, \qquad \Delta_{s,s}g=0. \end{equation}
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- definition-6: body_md -->
\label{def:Jrs} For distinct indices \(r\) and \(s\), define \begin{equation} \label{eq:Jrs} J_{r,s} = \{1,\ldots,k\} \setminus \{r,s\}. \end{equation}
<!-- end definition-6 -->
<!-- theorem-5: body_md -->
\label{thm:spectral-product-rule} 
Let \[ r,s\in\{1,\ldots,k\}, \qquad r\neq s. \] Then, for every admissible pair of functions \(f\) and \(g\), 
\begin{align} \label{eq:spectral-product-rule} 
\mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{U}}(fg) ={}& T_{\lambda_r}f\,\mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{U}} g + T_{\lambda_s}g\,\mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{U}} f + \frac1x \sum_{j\in J_{r,s}} A_j \Delta_{j,r}f \, \Delta_{j,s}g - \frac{\mathrm{U}_0}{x} T_{\lambda_r}f T_{\lambda_s}g.
\end{align}
<!-- end theorem-5 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
Define 
\begin{equation} \label{eq:auxiliary-sum-product-rule} 
S_{r,s}(f,g) = \sum_{j=1}^{k} A_j \Delta_{j,r}f \Delta_{j,s}g . 
\end{equation} 
Using the definitions of the spectral increments, 
\begin{align} 
S_{r,s}(f,g) = \sum_{j=1}^{k} A_j \bigl( T_{\lambda_j}f - T_{\lambda_r}f \bigr) \bigl( T_{\lambda_j}g - T_{\lambda_s}g \bigr). \label{eq:expanded-product-rule} 
\end{align} 
Expanding the product gives 
\begin{align} 
S_{r,s}(f,g) ={}& \sum_{j=1}^{k} A_j T_{\lambda_j}f T_{\lambda_j}g  - T_{\lambda_s}g \sum_{j=1}^{k} A_j T_{\lambda_j}f  - T_{\lambda_r}f \sum_{j=1}^{k} A_j T_{\lambda_j}g + T_{\lambda_r}f T_{\lambda_s}g \sum_{j=1}^{k} A_j . \label{eq:expanded-Srs} 
\end{align} 
Since $\sum_{j=1}^{k} A_jT_{\lambda_j}h = x\,\mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{U}} h, $ for every admissible function \(h\), and $ \sum_{j=1}^{k} A_j = \mathrm{U}_0, $ equation \eqref{eq:expanded-Srs} becomes \begin{align} 
S_{r,s}(f,g) = x\mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{U}}(fg) - xT_{\lambda_s}g\,\mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{U}} f - xT_{\lambda_r}f\,\mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{U}} g + \mathrm{U}_0 T_{\lambda_r}f T_{\lambda_s}g . \end{align} Solving for \(\mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{U}}(fg)\) yields 
\begin{align} 
\mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{U}}(fg) = T_{\lambda_r}f\,\mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{U}} g + T_{\lambda_s}g\,\mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{U}} f + \frac1x S_{r,s}(f,g) - \frac{\mathrm{U}_0}{x} T_{\lambda_r}f T_{\lambda_s}g . \label{eq:before-Jrs-reduction} 
\end{align} 
Now observe that \[ \Delta_{r,r}f=0, \qquad \Delta_{s,s}g=0. \] Hence the terms corresponding to \(j=r\) and \(j=s\) vanish identically in \eqref{eq:auxiliary-sum-product-rule}. Therefore \[ S_{r,s}(f,g) = \sum_{j\in J_{r,s}} A_j \Delta_{j,r}f \Delta_{j,s}g . \] Substituting this expression into \eqref{eq:before-Jrs-reduction} gives \eqref{eq:spectral-product-rule}.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- proposition-8: body_md -->
\label{prop:ward-product-rule} 
Assume that \(\mathrm{U}_0=0. \) Then 
\begin{align} \label{eq:ward-product-rule} 
\mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{U}}(fg) ={}& T_{\lambda_r}f\,\mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{U}} g + T_{\lambda_s}g\,\mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{U}} f + \frac1x \sum_{j\in J_{r,s}} A_j \Delta_{j,r}f \Delta_{j,s}g . 
\end{align}
<!-- end proposition-8 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
The result follows immediately from Theorem~\ref{thm:spectral-product-rule}, since the term \[ - \frac{\mathrm{U}_0}{x} T_{\lambda_r}f T_{\lambda_s}g \] vanishes identically when \(\mathrm{U}_0=0\).
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- corollary-7: body_md -->
\label{cor:product-rule-decomposition} 
The product rule \eqref{eq:spectral-product-rule} decomposes uniquely as 
\begin{equation} \label{eq:product-rule-decomposition} 
\mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{U}}(fg) = L_{r,s}(f,g) + I_{r,s}(f,g) + C_{r,s}(f,g), 
\end{equation} where 
\begin{align} 
L_{r,s}(f,g) &= T_{\lambda_r}f\,\mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{U}} g + T_{\lambda_s}g\,\mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{U}} f, \\ I_{r,s}(f,g) &= \frac1x \sum_{j\in J_{r,s}} A_j \Delta_{j,r}f \Delta_{j,s}g, \\ C_{r,s}(f,g) &= - \frac{\mathrm{U}_0}{x} T_{\lambda_r}f T_{\lambda_s}g. 
\end{align}
<!-- end corollary-7 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
This is merely a regrouping of the three terms appearing in Theorem~\ref{thm:spectral-product-rule}.
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- proposition-9: body_md -->
\label{prop:number-spectral-channels} 
For a recurrence sequence of order \(k\), the interaction term contains exactly $k-2$ spectral channels.
<!-- end proposition-9 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
By Definition~\ref{def:Jrs}, 
\[ 
J_{r,s} = \{1,\ldots,k\} \setminus \{r,s\}. 
\] 
Since the indices \(r\) and \(s\) are distinct, \(|J_{r,s}| = k-2. \) The interaction term contains precisely one summand for each element of \(J_{r,s}\). Hence the number of spectral interaction channels is \(k-2\).
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- corollary-8: body_md -->
\label{cor:order-two-product-rule} 
Assume that \(k=2\). Let the characteristic roots be \(\lambda_1,\lambda_2, \) and choose \( \{r,s\} = \{1,2\}. \) Then \begin{equation} \label{eq:order-two-product-rule} \mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{U}}(fg) = T_{\lambda_r}f\,\mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{U}} g + T_{\lambda_s}g\,\mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{U}} f - \frac{\mathrm{U}_0}{x} T_{\lambda_r}f T_{\lambda_s}g. 
\end{equation}
<!-- end corollary-8 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
If \(k=2\), then \(J_{r,s} = \varnothing. \) Therefore the interaction term in Theorem~\ref{thm:spectral-product-rule} vanishes identically. The result follows immediately.
<!-- end proof-17 -->
<!-- corollary-9: body_md -->
\label{cor:order-two-ward} Assume that \(k=2\) and \(\mathrm{U}_0=0. \) Then 
\begin{equation} \label{eq:order-two-ward} 
\mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{U}}(fg) = T_{\lambda_r}f\,\mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{U}} g + T_{\lambda_s}g\,\mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{U}} f. \end{equation}
<!-- end corollary-9 -->
<!-- corollary-10: body_md -->
\label{cor:order-three-product-rule} 
Assume that \(k=3\). Let \(\{r,s,\ell\} = \{1,2,3\}. \) Then \begin{align} \label{eq:order-three-product-rule} 
\mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{U}}(fg) ={}& T_{\lambda_r}f\,\mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{U}} g + T_{\lambda_s}g\,\mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{U}} f  + \frac{A_{\ell}}{x} \Delta_{\ell,r}f \Delta_{\ell,s}g - \frac{\mathrm{U}_0}{x} T_{\lambda_r}f T_{\lambda_s}g. 
\end{align}
<!-- end corollary-10 -->
<!-- proof-18: body_md -->
If \(k=3\), then \(J_{r,s} = \{\ell\}. \) Hence the interaction sum appearing in Theorem~\ref{thm:spectral-product-rule} contains exactly one term: \[ \sum_{j\in J_{r,s}} A_j \Delta_{j,r}f \Delta_{j,s}g = A_{\ell} \Delta_{\ell,r}f \Delta_{\ell,s}g. \] Substituting into \eqref{eq:spectral-product-rule} gives \eqref{eq:order-three-product-rule}.
<!-- end proof-18 -->
<!-- corollary-11: body_md -->
\label{cor:order-four-product-rule} 
Assume that \(k=4\). Let \(J_{r,s}=\{p,q\}. \) Then 
\begin{align} 
\mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{U}}(fg) ={}& T_{\lambda_r}f\,\mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{U}} g + T_{\lambda_s}g\,\mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{U}} f + \frac1x \Big( A_p\Delta_{p,r}f\Delta_{p,s}g + A_q\Delta_{q,r}f\Delta_{q,s}g \Big)\\
& - \frac{\mathrm{U}_0}{x} T_{\lambda_r}f T_{\lambda_s}g . \nonumber 
\end{align}
<!-- end corollary-11 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
Order four is the first order for which distinct interaction channels may cancel each other. This phenomenon does not occur in orders two and three.
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- proposition-10: body_md -->
\label{prop:monomial-product-identity} 
For every \(m,n\geq0\), 
\begin{align} \label{eq:monomial-product-identity} 
\mathrm{U}_{m+n} ={}& \lambda_r^{m}\mathrm{U}_n + \lambda_s^{n}\mathrm{U}_m - \mathrm{U}_0 \lambda_r^{m} \lambda_s^{n} + \sum_{j\in J_{r,s}} A_j \bigl( \lambda_j^{m} - \lambda_r^{m} \bigr) \bigl( \lambda_j^{n} - \lambda_s^{n} \bigr).
\end{align}
<!-- end proposition-10 -->
<!-- proof-19: body_md -->
Let \(f(x)=x^m\), \(g(x)=x^n. \) Then \(fg=x^{m+n}. \) By the fundamental monomial identity, \[ \mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{U}}(fg) = \mathrm{U}_{m+n}x^{m+n-1}. \] Moreover, 
\[ T_{\lambda_r}f = \lambda_r^m x^m, \qquad T_{\lambda_s}g = \lambda_s^n x^n, \] 
and 
\[ \mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{U}}(x^m) = \mathrm{U}_mx^{m-1}, \qquad \mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{U}}(x^n) = \mathrm{U}_nx^{n-1}. \] 
Substituting these expressions into Theorem~\ref{thm:spectral-product-rule} gives 
\begin{align} 
\mathrm{U}_{m+n}x^{m+n-1} ={}& \lambda_r^m\mathrm{U}_nx^{m+n-1} + \lambda_s^n\mathrm{U}_mx^{m+n-1} - \mathrm{U}_0 \lambda_r^m \lambda_s^n x^{m+n-1}\\ & + \sum_{j\in J_{r,s}} A_j (\lambda_j^m-\lambda_r^m) (\lambda_j^n-\lambda_s^n) x^{m+n-1}. \nonumber \end{align} Dividing by \(x^{m+n-1}\) yields \eqref{eq:monomial-product-identity}.
<!-- end proof-19 -->
<!-- corollary-12: body_md -->
\label{cor:order-two-addition} 
Assume that \(k=2\). Then 
\begin{equation} \label{eq:order-two-addition} \mathrm{U}_{m+n} = \lambda_r^m\mathrm{U}_n + \lambda_s^n\mathrm{U}_m - \mathrm{U}_0 \lambda_r^m \lambda_s^n . \end{equation}
<!-- end corollary-12 -->
<!-- corollary-13: body_md -->
\label{cor:order-two-ward-addition} 
Assume that \(k=2, \mathrm{U}_0=0. \) Then 
\begin{equation} \label{eq:order-two-ward-addition} 
\mathrm{U}_{m+n} = \lambda_r^m\mathrm{U}_n + \lambda_s^n\mathrm{U}_m. 
\end{equation}
<!-- end corollary-13 -->
<!-- remark-3: body_md -->
The identity \eqref{eq:monomial-product-identity} reveals a duality between the operator and the recurrence sequence. The spectral product rule determines an addition law for the recurrence coefficients, while the recurrence coefficients determine the monomial action of the operator through \[ \mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{U}} x^n=\mathrm{U}_nx^{n-1}. \] The operator and the recurrence therefore encode the same spectral information in two different forms.
<!-- end remark-3 -->
<!-- definition-7: body_md -->
\label{def:leibniz-defect} 
Let \[ r,s\in\{1,\ldots,k\}, \qquad r\neq s. \] The \((r,s)\)-Leibniz defect of an admissible pair of functions \((f,g)\) is defined by 
\begin{equation} \label{eq:leibniz-defect} 
\mathcal E_{r,s}(f,g) = \mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{U}}(fg) - T_{\lambda_r}f\,\mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{U}} g - T_{\lambda_s}g\,\mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{U}} f. \end{equation}
<!-- end definition-7 -->
<!-- proposition-11: body_md -->
\label{prop:defect-expression} 
For every admissible pair of functions \(f\) and \(g\), 
\begin{align} \label{eq:defect-expression} 
\mathcal E_{r,s}(f,g) = {}& \frac1x \sum_{j\in J_{r,s}} A_j \Delta_{j,r}f \Delta_{j,s}g - \frac{\mathrm{U}_0}{x} T_{\lambda_r}f T_{\lambda_s}g . 
\end{align}
<!-- end proposition-11 -->
<!-- proof-20: body_md -->
Subtracting \[ T_{\lambda_r}f\,\mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{U}} g + T_{\lambda_s}g\,\mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{U}} f \] from both sides of Theorem~\ref{thm:spectral-product-rule} gives \eqref{eq:defect-expression}.
<!-- end proof-20 -->
<!-- remark-4: body_md -->
The Leibniz defect is identically zero if and only if the spectral product rule reduces to the two-term identity \[ \mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{U}}(fg) = T_{\lambda_r}f\,\mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{U}} g + T_{\lambda_s}g\,\mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{U}} f. \] Consequently, the study of the multiplicative structure of \(\mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{U}}\) is equivalent to the study of the corresponding defect.
<!-- end remark-4 -->
<!-- theorem-6: body_md -->
\label{thm:zero-defect-criterion} 
Let \(r\neq s\). For an admissible pair of functions \((f,g)\), the following statements are equivalent: 
\begin{enumerate} 
\item \[ \mathcal E_{r,s}(f,g)=0; \] 
\item 
\begin{equation} \label{eq:general-zero-defect-condition} 
\sum_{j\in J_{r,s}} A_j \Delta_{j,r}f \Delta_{j,s}g = \mathrm{U}_0 T_{\lambda_r}f T_{\lambda_s}g. 
\end{equation} 
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end theorem-6 -->
<!-- proof-21: body_md -->
By Proposition~\ref{prop:defect-expression}, \[ \mathcal E_{r,s}(f,g) = \frac1x \sum_{j\in J_{r,s}} A_j \Delta_{j,r}f \Delta_{j,s}g - \frac{\mathrm{U}_0}{x} T_{\lambda_r}f T_{\lambda_s}g. \] Therefore \[ \mathcal E_{r,s}(f,g)=0 \] if and only if \[ \frac1x \sum_{j\in J_{r,s}} A_j \Delta_{j,r}f \Delta_{j,s}g = \frac{\mathrm{U}_0}{x} T_{\lambda_r}f T_{\lambda_s}g. \] Multiplication by \(x\) yields \eqref{eq:general-zero-defect-condition}. The converse follows by reversing the argument.
<!-- end proof-21 -->
<!-- corollary-14: body_md -->
\label{cor:zero-defect-equation} 
The pair \((f,g)\) satisfies the two-term spectral Leibniz identity 
\begin{equation} \label{eq:two-term-spectral-leibniz} 
\mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{U}}(fg) = T_{\lambda_r}f\,\mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{U}} g + T_{\lambda_s}g\,\mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{U}} f 
\end{equation} 
if and only if \eqref{eq:general-zero-defect-condition} holds.
<!-- end corollary-14 -->
<!-- proof-22: body_md -->
By Definition~\ref{def:leibniz-defect}, equation~\eqref{eq:two-term-spectral-leibniz} is equivalent to \[ \mathcal E_{r,s}(f,g)=0. \] The conclusion therefore follows immediately from Theorem~\ref{thm:zero-defect-criterion}.
<!-- end proof-22 -->
<!-- proposition-12: body_md -->
\label{prop:ward-defect} 
Assume that \(\mathrm{U}_0=0. \) Then 
\begin{equation} \label{eq:ward-defect} 
\mathcal E_{r,s}(f,g) = \frac1x \sum_{j\in J_{r,s}} A_j \Delta_{j,r}f \Delta_{j,s}g. 
\end{equation}
<!-- end proposition-12 -->
<!-- proof-23: body_md -->
By Proposition~\ref{prop:defect-expression}, \[ \mathcal E_{r,s}(f,g) = \frac1x \sum_{j\in J_{r,s}} A_j \Delta_{j,r}f \Delta_{j,s}g - \frac{\mathrm{U}_0}{x} T_{\lambda_r}f T_{\lambda_s}g. \] 
Since \(\mathrm{U}_0=0, \) the second term vanishes identically, yielding \eqref{eq:ward-defect}.
<!-- end proof-23 -->
<!-- corollary-15: body_md -->
\label{cor:ward-zero-defect} 
Assume that \(\mathrm{U}_0=0. \) Then \( \mathcal E_{r,s}(f,g)=0 \) if and only if 
\begin{equation} \label{eq:ward-zero-defect-condition} 
\sum_{j\in J_{r,s}} A_j \Delta_{j,r}f \Delta_{j,s}g = 0. 
\end{equation}
<!-- end corollary-15 -->
<!-- proof-24: body_md -->
Combining Theorem~\ref{thm:zero-defect-criterion} with the identity \(\mathrm{U}_0=0 \) gives \eqref{eq:ward-zero-defect-condition}.
<!-- end proof-24 -->
<!-- proposition-13: body_md -->
\label{prop:spectral-orthogonality-formula} 
Assume that \(\mathrm{U}_0=0. \) Then 
\begin{equation} \label{eq:defect-orthogonality} 
\mathcal E_{r,s}(f,g) = \frac1x \langle V_r f, V_s g \rangle_A. 
\end{equation}
<!-- end proposition-13 -->
<!-- proof-25: body_md -->
Substituting \eqref{eq:Vr-definition}, \eqref{eq:Vs-definition}, and \eqref{eq:weighted-bilinear-form} into \eqref{eq:ward-defect} yields \eqref{eq:defect-orthogonality}.
<!-- end proof-25 -->
<!-- corollary-16: body_md -->
\label{cor:spectral-orthogonality-criterion} 
Assume that \(\mathrm{U}_0=0. \) Then \(\mathcal E_{r,s}(f,g)=0 \) if and only if 
\begin{equation} \label{eq:spectral-orthogonality} 
\langle V_r f, V_s g \rangle_A = 0. 
\end{equation}
<!-- end corollary-16 -->
<!-- proof-26: body_md -->
By Proposition~\ref{prop:spectral-orthogonality-formula}, \[ \mathcal E_{r,s}(f,g) = \frac1x \langle V_r f, V_s g \rangle_A. \] Thus the defect vanishes exactly when the weighted inner product is zero.
<!-- end proof-26 -->
<!-- proposition-14: body_md -->
\label{prop:nonward-defect} 
Assume that \(\mathrm{U}_0\neq0. \) Then 
\begin{equation} \label{eq:nonward-defect} 
\mathcal E_{r,s}(f,g) = \frac1x \sum_{j\in J_{r,s}} A_j \Delta_{j,r}f \Delta_{j,s}g - \frac{\mathrm{U}_0}{x} T_{\lambda_r}f T_{\lambda_s}g. \end{equation}
<!-- end proposition-14 -->
<!-- proof-27: body_md -->
The identity follows directly from Proposition~\ref{prop:defect-expression} under the assumption \(\mathrm{U}_0\neq0. \)
<!-- end proof-27 -->
<!-- corollary-17: body_md -->
\label{cor:nonward-zero-defect} 
Assume that \(\mathrm{U}_0\neq0. \) Then 
\(\mathcal E_{r,s}(f,g)=0 \) if and only if 
\begin{equation} \label{eq:nonward-balance} 
\sum_{j\in J_{r,s}} A_j \Delta_{j,r}f \Delta_{j,s}g = \mathrm{U}_0 T_{\lambda_r}f T_{\lambda_s}g. 
\end{equation}
<!-- end corollary-17 -->
<!-- proof-28: body_md -->
This is the specialization of Theorem~\ref{thm:zero-defect-criterion} to the case \(\mathrm{U}_0\neq0. \)
<!-- end proof-28 -->
<!-- remark-5: body_md -->
\label{rem:spectral-balance} The vanishing of the Leibniz defect is governed by two fundamentally different mechanisms: \[ \text{Ward} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \text{spectral cancellation}, \] \[ \text{non-Ward} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \text{spectral balance}. \] The first requires the residual interaction channels to annihilate each other. The second requires those channels to compensate exactly for the initial-value contribution produced by \(\mathrm{U}_0\).
<!-- end remark-5 -->
<!-- theorem-7: body_md -->
Assume \[ T_{\lambda_r}g\neq0, \qquad T_{\lambda_s}g\neq0. \] Then \[ D_U\!\left(\frac{f}{g}\right) = \frac{ T_{\lambda_r}g\,D_Uf - T_{\lambda_r}f\,D_Ug - T_{\lambda_r}g\,\mathcal L_{r,s}(f/g,g) }{ T_{\lambda_r}g\, T_{\lambda_s}g }. \]
<!-- end theorem-7 -->
<!-- corollary-18: body_md -->
If \[ \mathcal L_{r,s}(f/g,g)=0, \] then \[ D_U\!\left(\frac{f}{g}\right) = \frac{ T_{\lambda_r}g\,D_Uf - T_{\lambda_r}f\,D_Ug }{ T_{\lambda_r}g\, T_{\lambda_s}g }. \]
<!-- end corollary-18 -->
<!-- definition-8: body_md -->
An elliptic non-Ward calculus is called singular when there exists an index \[ m>0 \] such that \[ b\sin(m\theta) = a\sin((m-1)\theta). \] Otherwise it is called regular.
<!-- end definition-8 -->
<!-- definition-9: body_md -->
An elliptic non-Ward calculus is called regular if \[ b\sin(n\theta) \neq a\sin((n-1)\theta) \] for every integer \(n\ge1\).
<!-- end definition-9 -->
<!-- theorem-8: body_md -->
\label{theo_CCSC}
Let \[ W_{n+2}=sW_{n+1}+tW_n \] be a nonzero second-order recurrence sequence and let \(\mathcal D_W\) denote its associated recurrence derivative. Then the calculus generated by \(W\) is completely determined by the triple \[ \bigl(W_0,\Delta,Z_W\bigr), \] where \[ \Delta=s^2+4t \] is the discriminant of the characteristic polynomial and \[ Z_W=\{n\ge 0:W_n=0\} \] is the zero set of the recurrence. More precisely: 
\begin{enumerate} \item The value \(W_0\) determines the primary bifurcation \[ W_0=0 \Longleftrightarrow \text{Ward calculus}, \qquad W_0\neq0 \Longleftrightarrow \text{non-Ward calculus}. \] \item The discriminant \(\Delta\) determines the spectral geometry: \[ \Delta>0 \Longrightarrow \text{hyperbolic}, \qquad \Delta=0 \Longrightarrow \text{parabolic}, \qquad \Delta<0 \Longrightarrow \text{elliptic}. \] \item The zero set \(Z_W\) determines the regularity type: \[ Z_W=\varnothing \Longrightarrow \text{regular}, \qquad Z_W\neq\varnothing \Longrightarrow \text{singular}. \] In the Ward case the index \(0\) is excluded from this test. 
\end{enumerate} 
Consequently, the classification problem for second-order recurrence calculi reduces to the determination of the three invariants \[ (W_0,\Delta,Z_W). \]
<!-- end theorem-8 -->
<!-- proof-29: body_md -->
The first assertion follows from the operator identity \[ \mathcal D_W(1)=W_0x^{-1}, \] which yields the Ward/non-Ward dichotomy. The second assertion follows from the classical classification of second-order recurrences according to the sign of the discriminant \(\Delta=s^2+4t\). The corresponding hyperbolic, parabolic and elliptic regimes were described in Sections~9.2 and~9.3. Finally, regularity and singularity are characterized by the presence or absence of additional zeros of the recurrence sequence. For Ward calculi this follows from the Lucas representations of Sections~9.2.1--9.2.3. For non-Ward calculi it follows from the Horadam zero criteria established in Sections~9.3.2 and~9.3.3. Since the three invariants \((W_0,\Delta,Z_W)\) are independent and each admits a unique value for a given recurrence, the resulting classification is exhaustive and mutually exclusive.
<!-- end proof-29 -->
<!-- corollary-19: body_md -->
For second-order recurrence calculi, the triple \[ (W_0,\Delta,Z_W) \] completely determines the qualitative regime of a second-order calculus
<!-- end corollary-19 -->
<!-- proof-30: body_md -->
Immediate from Theorem \ref{theo_CCSC}.
<!-- end proof-30 -->
<!-- remark-6: body_md -->
The singular and parabolic subclasses appear in this section only because completeness of the second-order classification requires their identification. The present paper does not attempt to develop the corresponding operator theories. In particular, the analysis of additional zero indices, the geometry of the zero set, nilpotent structures, truncation phenomena, and the operator calculus associated with repeated characteristic roots lies beyond the scope of this work. Nevertheless, these exceptional subclasses play an important conceptual role: they reveal the boundary of validity of the distinct-root theory and provide a first indication of the singular and confluent calculi that arise naturally from the recurrence-operator framework. Their systematic study will be developed in future work.
<!-- end remark-6 -->
